extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Montaigne, literature and philosophy readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria for philosophical inquiry and for representing the world, as expressed in Montaigne's essay — e.g., limits of human reason, distrust of authority, avoidance of anthropomorphism, and demands for practical accuracy in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of human reason in metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis Socrates’s opinion, and mine too, that the best judging of heaven is not to judge of it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate intellectual humility: refrain from asserting certainty about transcendent or celestial matters that lie beyond human senses and capacities. Treat grand metaphysical claims as beyond reliable human reach; prefer withholding judgment rather than making confident but unfounded assertions. (Anti-pattern: constructing elaborate, definitive accounts of the divine or heaven.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphism in theology
rubrics_metrics.description: It is so imprinted in our minds, and the fancy is so prepossessed with it, that when a man thinks of God, a human figure ever presents itself to the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not project human shape, passions, or needs onto the divine simply because imagination and familiarity incline us to do so. Recognize that likenesses drawn from ourselves reflect our perspective, not evidence about the divine. Example/anti-pattern: assuming gods must resemble humans because humans consider human form ‘the most beautiful’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat philosophical models as provisional inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy presents us not that which really is, or what she really believes, but what she has contrived with the greatest and most plausible likelihood of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand theories (e.g., epicycles, atoms, mechanistic images) as constructed, plausible explanations rather than final truths. Use them as working tools, and remain open to revision. (Anti-pattern: taking elaborate theoretical contrivances as literal reality.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Question authority and received doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The god of scholastic knowledge is Aristotle; ‘tis irreligion to question any of his decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept claims solely on the basis of authoritative status. Examine foundational premises rather than deferring to magisterial authors. Where scholars build whole systems on presuppositions, those presuppositions should themselves be open to scrutiny. (Scoring note: high value placed on independent critical inquiry.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate root causes rather than superficial branches
rubrics_metrics.description: They do not dig to the root, where the faults and defects lie; they only debate upon the branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanations, prioritize examination of fundamental assumptions and origins over debating peripheral consequences or formulations. Avoid getting lost in sophistical refinements while ignoring core uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value practical, observable knowledge over abstruse speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates... thought it was enough to know so much of geometry only as to measure the land a man bought or sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer knowledge with practical applicability and clear sensory grounding. Be wary of seeking abstruse truths with little bearing on ordinary life. (Example: geometry useful for land-measurement vs. speculative celestial mechanics without observable grounding.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of presuppositional reasoning and closed systems
rubrics_metrics.description: For every science has its principle presupposed, by which human judgment is everywhere kept in check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and test the a priori assumptions underlying disciplinary systems (axioms, first principles). Recognize that different foundational choices can lead to equally coherent but incompatible systems; therefore, compare and weigh foundational premises rather than only their derived conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let imagination assimilate other things to one's own kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing assimilates the qualities of all other things to its own proper qualities... our imagination cannot go beyond it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting nature or other minds, resist the tendency to explain unfamiliar phenomena by projecting familiar qualities. Acknowledge the limits of analogy and the risk of self-centered bias in explanation (anti-pattern: assuming all beings would make gods like themselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand accuracy in representation of familiar subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: When they come and draw us after life, or any other creature which is known and familiar to us, we then require of them a perfect and exact representation of lineaments and colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards for depiction: representations of well-known, familiar things must be precise and faithful; greater tolerance for vagueness is allowed only when representing remote or unknown subjects. (Application: painters, writers, and philosophers should be held to higher exactitude when describing ordinary, observable things.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize poetic/metaphorical elements in philosophical discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy is no other than sophisticated poetry. Whence do the ancient writers extract their authorities but from the poets?... Plato is but a poet unripped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to metaphor, allegory, and poetic style embedded in philosophical writing; interpret such passages as rhetorical or illustrative rather than literal expositions of empirical fact. Distinguish poetic argument from demonstrative proof to avoid taking figurative language as scientific description.
